newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan market cheers reform income tax at 25 pct.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan market cheers reform income tax at 25 pct.

text.p: The stock market on Thursday hailed a key reform unifying Taiwan's two income taxes, but experts said the government, which acquiesced to pressure to keep the levy low, would have to scramble to recoup lost revenue.

The Finance Ministry confirmed it had agreed to fix the merged business income tax rate at 25 percent, abandoning a drive to squeeze out a tax windfall and avert a drop in state revenues by setting the rate at 35 percent.
The compromise, which had been aggressively promoted by commercial interests, sent the stock market surging to a 1.12 percent gain in active turnover.

"The news gave the market a definite boost, as most businesses had been against a tax rise," said Nikko Securities analyst Michael Hung. "But it remains to be seen how the government decides to make up the lost tax revenue."

Businesses have complained that Taiwan's dual system, where earnings are subject to a business income tax and a personal income tax, was cumbersome and unfair. The personal income tax is 40 percent for the highest brackets while the current business income tax is 25 percent.

A ministry official reached by telephone said a merger of the old business income tax and personal income tax would not be formally announced until October 11 and said a change in the compromise tax rate before then was possible, though unlikely.

He said objections from business groups forced the ministry to give up hopes of setting the merged tax at 35 percent, which would have yielded revenues similar to those under the dual system plus a T$4.6 billion (US$167 million) annual windfall.
Experts from a blue-ribbon tax reform committee said the compromise could not be avoided.

"The finance ministry must compromise," said Sun Ke-nan, a panel member from the Chunghua Institution for Economic Research. "Otherwise parliament, under heavy pressure from the business, will not pass the proposal."

Economist Sun said a 25 percent tax rate would reduce state revenues by T$26.8 billion (US$975 million) a year and even a rate of 30 percent, which has been suggested by some, would trim revenues by T$11 billion (US$400 million).

Sun said the tax commission had suggested three ways to recoup the tax losses -- cutting government spending, increasing the value-added tax or levying a 10 percent business income tax on enterprises' reserved profits.
"Reducing spending 5-6 percent through more efficient management should help cover the expected loss," Sun said.
"Adding one percentage point to the five percent value-added tax would increase income by some T$40-50 billion (US$1.45-1.82 billion), but this might cause inflation," he said.
